My grandmother wrote letters. Real ones, on paper, and if you lived abroad you waited a fortnight for the reply. I thought about that last week when my cousin in Melbourne video-called me to show off her new kitchen and the lag was so small I could watch her roll her eyes in real time. That's the thing about modern technology: it stopped feeling like technology a while ago. It's just the plumbing of ordinary life now.

The communication shift is the obvious one, and everyone has their own version of the Melbourne kitchen story. WhatsApp groups for the extended family. A relative patched into a funeral over Zoom because the flights were impossible. What interests me more than the speed is the texture — you can keep a low-grade, everyday intimacy with someone on another continent, the kind that used to require living on the same street.

Money is the quieter revolution. A freelance illustrator I know works from a town of 4,000 people and has clients in three time zones; twenty years ago she'd have moved to a city or changed careers. Mobile money did something similar at far larger scale — Kenya's M-Pesa turned a basic phone into a bank branch for millions of people the formal system had ignored. Online courses did it for education, though completion rates tell a less flattering story than the marketing. Access isn't follow-through, but access is where it starts.

Health is where the stakes sit highest. Screening software now catches diabetic retinopathy early enough to save sight in clinics that have no specialist and never will. My watch buzzes when my heart rate does something odd while I'm sitting still. Slightly creepy? Sure. But it flagged an arrhythmia in a friend who didn't know she had one, so I've made my peace with creepy.

Then there's the boring stuff, which might matter most in aggregate. I haven't queued in a bank in years. Bills pay themselves. I don't get lost driving anymore — I get annoyed when the GPS adds four minutes. None of this is impressive alone, but across a week it buys back hours that used to go to errands, hours that now go to kids, hobbies, sleep, or (let's be honest) more screen time.

And that is the caveat. Attention spans have taken a visible beating, mine included. The privacy trade-offs are real and mostly unread. And none of this levelling helps the person who can't afford a decent connection. Technology amplifies what's already there; it doesn't fix it.

So the question isn't whether technology belongs at the centre of daily life — that ship sailed, and it was carrying smartphones. It's whether we stay awake at the wheel, using these tools on purpose instead of letting the defaults decide. On current evidence, the jury is very much out.
